summary: Adding or subtracting two numbers stated in a short word problem.
description: A one- or two-sentence story (money, lives saved, plain numbers) gives two integers, decimals or large numbers and implies an addition or a subtraction. The model picks the exact result from four numeric options; distractors include the result of the wrong operation and off-by-one or off-by-ten values.
example: You received a gift card and made a purchase. Calculate how much is still left in the gift card: $33.53 - $21.97

summary: Multiplying or dividing two numbers, including negative numbers, stated in a short word problem.
description: A short prompt gives two numbers (positive, negative or one of each) and asks for their product or quotient, sometimes inside a story about rent, prices or quantities. The correct option is the exact result rounded to two decimals; the question states the rounding; distractors (all within a factor of 3 of the answer) are sign errors, digit slips and the other operation where it is of similar size.
example: A math competition question asks you to solve the following problem quickly. What is -63 divided by -43?

summary: Computing the expected value of a simple random experiment such as a coin flip, die roll or draw from a bag.
description: The question describes a random event with stated payoffs or probabilities (coins, dice, bags of items, weather) and asks for its expected value; some items have negative payoffs and some ask for an expected number of draws. Coins and dice are stated to be fair. The model picks the correctly computed expectation from four options with matching units, all within the range of possible outcomes.
example: Upon flipping a coin, heads will give you 23 points while tails will deduct 38 points. Determine the expected value of this action.

summary: Comparing or computing the probabilities of simple events, including recognising equal probabilities written in different formats.
description: Four kinds of question, all with exact keys. Same probability (Yes/No): two sources (weather services, sports analysts, fair stalls, clinical studies) state a probability in two different formats, among 0.35, 35%, 7/20 and "7 in 20"; the values are equal in half of the questions and otherwise differ by 0.05 to 0.15 or by a factor of ten (0.4 against 4%). Most likely / least likely: two or three events, each a separate experiment with a fair die, two fair dice, fair coins, a standard 52-card deck, or two or three bags with stated marble counts; the probabilities are distinct and the answer is at least 0.02 ahead of the next. Compute: the probability of one event (13 with one die, 12 with two dice, 11 with two coin flips, 12 with three, 18 with one card, each with two wordings of the setup; or a marble from a bag with stated counts), with four reduced fractions as options: the key and three wrong values from common mistakes (the complement, favourable over unfavourable outcomes, one count off, double or half). The wrong values depend only on the event, so a repeated question always has the same options.
example: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that both dice show an even number? [options: 1/4 / 1/3 / 3/4 / 2/9]

summary: Using the complement rule to find the probability of the remaining outcome when the others are given.
description: A scenario gives the probability of one outcome, or of two disjoint outcomes, and asks for the probability of the remaining one. The correct option is one minus the sum of the given probabilities. Most questions have three numeric options (about 10% have two); the distractors are other nearby probabilities.
example: You are playing a lottery and there are two possible outcomes: win or lose. The probability 0.46 is the chance that you win, and the probability 0.22 is the chance that you don't play. What is the probability that you lose?

summary: Applying Bayes' rule to compute a conditional probability from a prior, a likelihood and a marginal.
description: Sports-themed questions give the probability of an event, the probability of the event under a condition, and the probability of the condition, then ask for the probability of the condition given that the event happened. The correct option is P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B), written as a percentage rounded to two decimals as the question asks; the distractors are common mistakes (inverting the conditional, the joint probability, leaving out the likelihood), at most one of them a number copied from the question.
example: Tony has a 39% chance of scoring a touchdown. In 11% of games when he is playing with Team A, he scores a touchdown. He plays with Team A 59% of the time. Tony just scored a touchdown, what is the probability he is playing with Team A?

summary: Deciding which conclusion must follow from two categorical premises ("All A are B", "Some B are not C").
description: A context sentence names a population (guests at a wedding, animals at a rescue centre, plants in a botanical garden, items in an antique shop, or made-up creatures such as wugs and blickets), then two premises in the forms All / No / Some / Some ... not, relating three groups in any of the four syllogistic figures. The question states that every group mentioned has at least one member and asks which conclusion must be true. The options are three conclusions about the two outer groups and "Cannot be determined." In half of the questions one listed conclusion must follow (the others listed do not); in the other half no conclusion relating the two outer groups follows, in either direction, and the key is "Cannot be determined." The groups are attributes that everyday knowledge does not relate (vaccinated and microchipped animals, wooden and imported items) or made-up words, so only the premises decide.
example: Consider the guests at a large wedding. All bakers are chess players. All swimmers are bakers. Assume that every group mentioned has at least one member. Solely from the information provided, which of the following must be true? [options: All swimmers are chess players. / No swimmers are chess players. / Some swimmers are not chess players. / Cannot be determined.]

summary: Deciding what follows from an if-then rule and a second premise, avoiding affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent.
description: A rule "If P, then Q" from a fixed bank of 39 (20 about a named man or woman: a first-class ticket and the airport lounge, a fever and staying home; 19 about events, numbers or shapes: rain and the picnic, a number divisible by 6 and an even number, a regular hexagon and six sides), followed by a second premise: P, not-Q, Q or not-P, in equal shares. The question asks which conclusion must be true. The options are the two clauses of the other part of the rule (for example "Clara can use the airport lounge." and "Clara cannot use the airport lounge.") and "Cannot be determined." The key is Q after P (modus ponens), not-P after not-Q (modus tollens), and "Cannot be determined." after Q (affirming the consequent) or not-P (denying the antecedent), so half the keys are "Cannot be determined." and the fallacious conclusion is always offered. The number and shape rules are true but their converses are not, so general knowledge never settles a fallacy. The type is the argument form.
example: If Omar works from home on Monday, then he joins the team meeting by video. Omar joins the team meeting by video. Based only on these statements, which conclusion follows? [options: Omar works from home on Monday. / Omar does not work from home on Monday. / Cannot be determined.]

summary: Recognising that a conditional statement is equivalent to its contrapositive.
description: A person or an expert asserts "if P, then Q" in an everyday, financial or medical setting (429 contexts, normalised by fixed rules). Most questions offer three options, about one in ten four: the contrapositive ("if not Q, then not P") and two or three of the converse ("if Q, then P"), the inverse ("if not P, then not Q") and the statement with its conclusion negated ("if P, then not Q"). Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent. Every option is built from the same four clauses as the statement (P, Q and their negations, each negation in the clause's own tense and with its own subject), so the key cannot be told apart by its wording.
example: A gastroenterologist suggests, "If the patient is suffering from celiac disease, then the patient will have a reaction to gluten." The logically equivalent statement is: [options: If the patient will have a reaction to gluten, then the patient is suffering from celiac disease. / If the patient is suffering from celiac disease, then the patient will not have a reaction to gluten. / If the patient will not have a reaction to gluten, then the patient is not suffering from celiac disease.; key the third]

summary: Predicting where a character will look for an object that was or was not moved in their sight.
description: Unexpected-transfer stories over ten fixed scenarios (a marble in a basket, a stapler in a drawer, a car key on a hook, a sun hat in a beach bag, ...): a character puts an object in one place, and someone moves it to another. In half of the questions the character is away and is not told, so the key is the original place (a false belief); in the other half the character watches through the window, stays in the room and sees the move, or reads a message from the mover saying where the object is now, so the key is the new place. The question asks where the character will look first or thinks the object is; the two options are the two places. Each story is told with a named mover or with the reader as the mover. Secret-keeping questions ("you were told something in confidence; what should you do?") are not included: what one should do is a norm, not something the story determines.
example: Nadia puts her marble in the basket and goes outside to play. While she is away, Samuel moves the marble to the toy box. Then Nadia comes back. Where will Nadia look for her marble first? [options: In the basket / In the toy box]

summary: Reasoning about where one character thinks another will look for an object that was moved twice, when the first may not know what the second has learned.
description: Unexpected-transfer stories over the ten scenarios of first_order_false_belief, with a third place for each. The owner puts an object in one place and leaves; an observer stays in the room and watches while a third person (or the reader) moves the object to a second place and later to a third. After each move the owner may learn of it openly (phoned in front of the observer), secretly (a message the observer does not know about), or not at all; after the second move the mover may also tell the observer, mistakenly, that the owner has been told. The question asks where the observer thinks the owner will look. In observer_wrong questions (five of the seven story variants) the observer's belief about the owner is false, so the key differs from where the owner will really look; in observer_right questions the observer is right but the owner is wrong, so the key differs from where the object is and from what the observer believes about it. Each of the three places is the key in about a third of the questions, so neither the place where the object was first put nor the place where it is answers the questions. Options are the three places. Third person, and second person with the reader as the mover.
example: Leila and Lucas are in the hallway. Leila puts her car key on the hook by the door and leaves to take a shower; Lucas stays in the hallway. While she is away, you come in and move the car key into the fruit bowl while Lucas watches. You also send Leila a message about this move, which Leila reads at once; Lucas does not know about the message. Later, you move the car key again, onto the kitchen table, and Lucas sees this too. Nobody tells Leila about the second move. When Leila returns, where does Lucas expect her to look for the car key first? [options: In the fruit bowl / On the kitchen table / On the hook by the door; key On the hook by the door]

module: Axioms of Utility in Deterministic Environments
summary: Choosing consistently with transitive preferences: if A is preferred to B and B to C, then A is preferred to C.
description: A short scene (job offers in several cities, a holiday country, fruit for a salad, a partner for a group project, a Saturday activity) followed by two or three stated pairwise preferences over three or four alternatives, in random order and worded four ways ("prefers A over B", "likes A more than B", "likes B less than A", "finds B less appealing than A"). The preferences form a chain, or with four alternatives a fork or a join. The two options are a pair that is never compared directly but is ordered by chaining the stated preferences; the question asks which of the two is preferred, or, in half of the questions, which is liked less. Pairs the statements leave unordered are never asked and no statements are cyclic. Each scene is told in the second person, about a named man or woman, and with the reader as an AI assistant acting for a named client.
example: Leila is choosing fruit for her fruit salad. Leila prefers mangoes over peaches. She finds apricots less appealing than peaches. She likes apricots more than papayas. Of the two options below, which does Leila prefer? [options: Peaches / Papayas]

module: Axioms of Utility in Deterministic Environments
summary: Making choices that are not changed by adding an irrelevant, dominated alternative (the decoy effect).
description: Each question has two parts, with scenario sentences recovered from the v1 decoy templates (1,074 everyday- and technological-product scenarios that name no attribute other than price and quality). Part 0 offers brands A and B with a price and a quality rating: one cheaper, the other better. Part 1 repeats A and B and adds brand C, the standard asymmetric decoy: worse than the target (A or B, at random) on both price and quality, but better than the other brand on one of them. Both parts also offer "No preference between Brand A and Brand B". Any part-0 choice is acceptable, but the part-1 choice must be the same (the same brand, or no preference again), and C is never a consistent choice.
example: You stumble upon two types of blenders at the electronics store. Which one will you buy? [options: Brand A: price is $410, with quality rating 33 / Brand B: price is $698, with quality rating 46] [part 1: You stumble upon three types of blenders at the electronics store. Which one will you buy? Adds: Brand C: price is $814, with quality rating 42]

module: Axioms of Utility in Deterministic Environments
summary: Stating a preference, or indifference, between every pair of four or five fully described alternatives instead of declining to choose.
description: Each question describes four or five alternatives, certain outcomes that trade off against each other (job offers, apartments, laptops, holiday packages, medical treatments, savings bonds), and says that the description is complete: the alternatives differ in nothing else and no more information is available. It has one part per pair of alternatives (6 or 10 parts); every part shows the same description and asks about one pair, with four options: prefer the first, prefer the second, indifferent, or "I cannot decide between X and Y". Any preference or indifference is acceptable and no option is correct. The parts are graded together: the answers are complete if no pair is answered "cannot decide". Whether the answered pairs are also transitive is reported besides. Second person (the reader's own preference).
example:
You are moving to a new city and can rent any of these apartments for a year:
Apartment A: rent of $2,250 a month, 70 square metres of floor space and 18 minutes' walk from the station.
Apartment B: rent of $2,300 a month, 95 square metres of floor space and 6 minutes' walk from the station.
Apartment C: rent of $2,350 a month, 85 square metres of floor space and 9 minutes' walk from the station.
Apartment D: rent of $1,450 a month, 90 square metres of floor space and 7 minutes' walk from the station.
These descriptions are complete: the apartments differ in nothing else, and no more information is available. Between Apartment A and Apartment B, which would you choose? [options: I prefer Apartment A / I prefer Apartment B / I am indifferent between Apartment A and Apartment B / I cannot decide between Apartment A and Apartment B; one part per pair (6 parts), graded together]

display_name: Avoidance of the Sunk Cost Fallacy
module: Avoidance of Cognitive Biases in Deterministic Environments
summary: Making forward-looking decisions that ignore costs already spent and unrecoverable.
description: Twenty fixed scenarios (an earbud prototype, a half-built hotel, a television campaign, a feature film, an apple orchard, a non-refundable retreat venue, a database migration by hand, ...), fifteen about money and five about hours. Each states the amount already spent and that it cannot be recovered, and for each course of action its further cost and future value: continue the original plan, switch to an alternative, or stop (no further cost, no further value). The key is the option with the highest future net value, at least three units of the scenario's scale ahead; it is continuing, switching or stopping, each a third of the time. When it is switching or stopping, counting the sunk amount as lost would make continuing look best (the sunk-cost trap); the sunk amount is drawn independently of the future values. Time savings are stated as totals over the coming year. When the key is continuing or switching, it costs more and is worth more than the other course (or less and less), so it does not win on both. Each scenario is told in the first, second and third person (a man, a woman) and with the reader as an AI assistant in charge of the decision.
example: You are an AI assistant in charge of a sportswear brand's advertising budget, and this decision is yours to make. You already spent $150,000 producing and airing the first half of a television campaign for the sportswear brand. Since then, most of the target audience has moved to streaming and social media. None of the $150,000 already spent can be recovered, whatever the decision. Running the rest of the television campaign would cost another $34,000 and bring in $9,000. Moving the campaign online would cost $37,000 and bring in $32,000. Ending the campaign would cost nothing more and bring in nothing. What should you do?

module: Avoidance of Cognitive Biases in Deterministic Environments
summary: Valuing a good the same whether or not you already own it, so mirrored trade offers get opposite answers.
description: Each question has two parts: the same short story told twice with the two items swapped. In part 0 you own item X and are offered item Y of the same stated value in exchange; in part 1 you own Y and are offered X. Each part stands on its own, says the exchange costs nothing and takes no effort, and is answered Yes, No or indifferent. The items are 30 fixed pairs of similar kind and price (a ceramic mug and a bar of Swiss chocolate, wireless earbuds and a portable speaker, tickets to a jazz concert and to a comedy show, ...), and the stories are a conference gift, a raffle prize, a present that the shop will exchange, a thank-you for a survey, a charity shop's stock managed by the reader as an AI assistant, and advice to a named man or woman. With a preference that does not depend on which item is owned, exactly one of the two offers is accepted, so Yes then No or No then Yes is consistent, and so is indifferent in both parts; No in both parts is the endowment effect.
example: You win a portable speaker in a raffle at work. A colleague who won a pair of wireless earbuds in the same raffle offers to trade prizes with you. Both prizes are worth about $85. Do you accept the trade? [options: Yes / No] [part 1: the same story with the speaker and the earbuds swapped]

module: Avoidance of Cognitive Biases in Deterministic Environments
summary: Keeping the same choice between a smaller-sooner and larger-later reward when both are pushed into the future.
description: The question states the agent's earlier choice between an amount today and a larger amount tomorrow, then offers the same two amounts shifted by many days (e.g. day 53 vs day 54). The keyed answer is the option that matches the earlier choice, as an exponential (time-consistent) discounter would choose.
example: Let's say when you were asked to make a choice between receiving $115 today or $133 tomorrow, you chose 115 dollars today. With that in mind would you rather receive 115 dollars in 53 days, or wait an extra day to receive $133 dollars?

paper_aliases.note: The 2024 STEER-ME data that the paper's heatmap reports as Exponential Discounting (exponential_discounting in the 2024 runs, 1,990 questions) were time-consistency questions of this design. The site's STEER-ME element of that name (present_value) asks for present values instead.

module: Axioms of Utility in Stochastic Environments
summary: Applying transitivity to preferences between lotteries.
description: Two stated preferences chain three lotteries (e.g. a 44% chance of X preferred to an 83% chance of Y, which is preferred to a 54% chance of Z). The model chooses among the transitive conclusion, its reverse and "Cannot determine preference"; the transitive conclusion is correct.
example: You have the following preferences over vacations: Preference X: A 44% chance of a mountain chalet vacation is preferred over a 83% chance of a beach resort vacation. Preference Y: A 83% chance of a beach resort vacation is preferred over a 54% chance of a vacation in a big city. Which of the following should you prefer?

module: Axioms of Utility in Stochastic Environments
summary: Applying the independence axiom: mixing two options with the same third lottery should not reverse the preference.
description: The agent prefers item A to item B. Option X gives A with probability p and C otherwise; Option Y gives B with probability p and the same C otherwise. The correct choice is Option X, the one built on the preferred item (sure-thing reasoning). The lottery with the preferred item is described first in half of the questions and second in the other half.
example: Suppose you have a preference for a laptop over a smartwatch. You're presented with the options: Option X - 90% chance at a laptop and a 10% chance at a smartphone, versus Option Y - 90% chance at a smartwatch and a 10% chance at a smartphone. Which option aligns with your preference?

module: Axioms of Utility in Stochastic Environments
summary: Stating a preference, or indifference, between every pair of four or five fully described lotteries instead of declining to choose.
description: Each question describes four or five alternatives, lotteries stated with exact chances (game-show envelopes, one-year investments, treatments with a chance of a faster recovery, bonus plans with three outcomes, crops whose earnings depend on the weather, travel routes with a chance of delay), and says that the description is complete: the alternatives differ in nothing else and no more information is available. It has one part per pair of alternatives (6 or 10 parts); every part shows the same description and asks about one pair, with four options: prefer the first, prefer the second, indifferent, or "I cannot decide between X and Y". Any preference or indifference is acceptable and no option is correct. The parts are graded together: the answers are complete if no pair is answered "cannot decide". Whether the answered pairs are also transitive is reported besides. Second person (the reader's own preference).
example:
You have won a game-show round and may pick one envelope. Each pays a random prize with these exact chances:
Envelope A: a 70% chance of $1,400 and otherwise $100.
Envelope B: a 90% chance of $1,100 and otherwise $400.
Envelope C: a 30% chance of $900 and otherwise $200.
Envelope D: a 30% chance of $1,700 and otherwise $400.
Envelope E: a 20% chance of $1,600 and otherwise $100.
These descriptions are complete: the envelopes differ in nothing else, and no more information is available. Between Envelope A and Envelope B, which would you choose? [options: I prefer Envelope A / I prefer Envelope B / I am indifferent between Envelope A and Envelope B / I cannot decide between Envelope A and Envelope B; one part per pair (10 parts), graded together]

summary: Computing the expected utility of a lottery from stated probabilities and utilities.
description: A treatment, job, vacation, investment or lottery has two or three outcomes with stated probabilities and utilities, and the question asks for its expected utility. The correct option is the probability-weighted sum of the utilities, shown among three numeric options; the distractors (unweighted mean, probabilities swapped) lie between the smallest and largest utility.
example: A patient has a 66% chance of recovery with Treatment A. The utility of recovery is 35, while the utility of not recovering is 0. Calculate the expected utility for Treatment A.

summary: Choosing the option with the highest expected value when utility is linear in money.
description: Each question states that the chooser's utility is linear in money and offers a sure amount and one or two lotteries with whole-percentage probabilities (game shows, casinos, contests), or two job offers: a sure salary, or a lower salary with a chance of a bonus. Every lottery has one outcome above and one below the sure amount; the key is the option with the highest expected value, which beats the others by at least 5% (2% for the job offers). Only this plain type is generated: the certainty and reflection framings are their own elements, and the loss-aversion framing is not used (Avoidance of Loss Averse Behavior has its own questions).
example: You are at a casino facing two betting options on a game. Your utility is linear in money: every dollar is worth the same to you, however much you already have. Which option maximizes your expected utility? [options: $448 with a 29% chance and $73 with a 71% chance / A guaranteed $410]

summary: Taking a mixed gamble with positive expected value despite a framing that invites loss-averse rejection.
description: Five stories (a coin-flip bet with a friend, a marketing campaign, a short-term trade, a game-show wheel, an optional bonus / deduction pay scheme) offer a gamble that wins $G with stated probability and otherwise loses $L of the decision maker's own money. The probability-weighted gain is 1.1 to 2 times the weighted loss, so the expected value is positive but a loss-averse chooser would reject. Every question says the decision maker faces many small decisions like this, the amounts are small compared with their savings, and they care about the average result. In accept_reject questions the alternative is doing nothing; in a third of them the gamble has a negative expected value (weighted gain 0.5 to 0.87 times the weighted loss) and declining is the key; in sure_amount questions it is a small guaranteed payment, which is the better choice in about a third of them. Six perspectives, including an AI assistant advising a client.
example: Arjun's employer offers an optional pay scheme for the next project: a bonus of $590 if the project finishes on time, which has a 30% chance, and a deduction of $140 from Arjun's pay if it does not. Arjun faces many small decisions like this one, and the amounts are small compared with Arjun's savings. What should Arjun do? [options: Stay on the standard pay / Join the scheme; key Join the scheme]

module: Avoidance of Cognitive Biases in Stochastic Environments
summary: Recognising that a streak of independent random outcomes does not change the odds of the next one.
description: After a streak at roulette, dice, slot machines, lotteries or with coin flips, the question asks whether the streak has made some outcome more (or less) likely on the next trial. Templates where "Yes" is defensible (a "different outcome" being more likely than the streak outcome), card games dealt from a shoe or deck (not independent), and questions with no comparison are not used. The correct answer is "No": independent draws keep the same probabilities.
example: Let's say you are at a roulette table and the ball has fallen on black 10 times in a row. Is the ball now more likely to fall on red than it was before?

module: Avoidance of Cognitive Biases in Stochastic Environments
summary: Choosing consistently across Allais-style lottery pairs, without overweighting outcomes that are certain.
description: Each question states an earlier choice between X for sure and Y with probability p, then offers X with probability k and Y with probability k*p (probabilities scaled by a common factor). The question says that the preferences have not changed since then. Under expected utility the new choice should be on the same side as the earlier one, so the keyed option is the scaled version of the option chosen before.
example: Earlier, Carlos was offered a choice between two protocols, "A protocol that is certain to save 98 lives" and "A protocol with a 60% chance of saving 188 lives, and none otherwise", and he chose "A protocol that is certain to save 98 lives". Now, Carlos is choosing how an intensive care unit will treat patients [...] Which of the following protocols should Carlos choose?

module: Avoidance of Cognitive Biases in Stochastic Environments
summary: Keeping the same risk attitude when a choice between gains is mirrored into a choice between losses.
description: Each question states an earlier choice between a sure gain X and a gain Y with probability p (equal expected value, p*Y = X), then offers the loss mirror: lose X for sure or have to pay Y with probability p. The question says that the earlier choice was a strict preference and the attitude to risk has not changed. With one strict risk attitude across gains and losses, the keyed option is on the same side (sure or risky) as the earlier choice.
example: Earlier, Aisha was offered a choice between two trades, "A trade that locks in a gain of $944 for certain" and "A trade with an 80% chance of a gain of $1,180, and no gain otherwise", and she chose "A trade with an 80% chance of a gain of $1,180, and no gain otherwise". Now, Aisha has an option trade that has moved against her [...] Which of the following exit strategies should Aisha choose?

module: Avoidance of Cognitive Biases in Stochastic Environments
summary: Making Ellsberg-urn choices that can be explained by a single belief about the unknown proportions.
description: Ellsberg's three-colour urn in two parts, recovered from the v1 templates (414 balls-and-urn and mythical-treasure templates; the 165 'goods' templates name no colours and were not used). The urn holds n items of a known colour and 2n of two other colours in unknown proportions (n = 1-100); every bet pays the same reward. Part 0: bet on the known colour or on one unknown colour. Part 1: bet on the two unknown colours together, or on the known colour plus the second unknown colour. Part 0 says one item is drawn at random, each equally likely. Each part also offers "Indifferent between the two options". A pair of choices is consistent if a single subjective probability justifies it: the known-probability bet in exactly one of the two parts, or indifferent in both (p = 1/3). The classic ambiguity-averse pattern (the known-probability bet in both parts) is inconsistent.
example: You are selecting from a container containing 144 balls. It has 48 green balls and 96 balls that are an enigmatic blend of blue or yellow. You have two choices: [options: Gain 4 dollars if you select a blue ball and 0 otherwise. / Gain 4 dollars if you pick a green ball and 0 otherwise] [part 1: Next, you are proposed a second scenario (with the same values as before). Options: Gain 4 dollars if you select a green or yellow ball and 0 otherwise. / Gain 4 dollars if you select a blue or yellow ball and 0 otherwise]

summary: Reading a payoff from a normal-form game matrix for a given pair of actions.
description: A small payoff matrix (yours or your opponent's) is given, with the model playing as the row or column player, and the question asks for a specific payoff when each player takes a named action. The correct option is the matching cell value.
example: Below, find your payoff matrix for some game. You are the column player What is your payoff if you play Action X and your opponent plays Action S? Action X Action Y Action R 7 6 Action S 9 7

summary: Finding a player's best response to a given action of the other player in a bimatrix game.
description: A 2x2 or 3x3 bimatrix game is shown and the model is told which player it is. The question asks for its own or its opponent's best response to a specified action of the other player. The correct option is the action with the highest payoff for the responding player in that row or column, among that player's two or three actions; games with ties are excluded.
example: Below, find the payoff matrix for some game. You are the column player, which means the second number in the cell is your payoff and the first is your opponent's, what action is your best response if your opponent plays Action T? [3x3 payoff matrix]

summary: Identifying and playing a dominant strategy in a two-player, two-action game described in words.
description: Two kinds of story, each built from a payoff table generated first. Pricing stories (symmetric and non-symmetric): two shops each charge a low or a high price, the story lists the units each sells in all four price combinations and states the objective, profit = price x units sold, each maximising its own. Negotiation stories: two new hires each negotiate or accept an offer; the story lists the raise each gets in all four combinations and says each wants the largest raise for themselves. The question asks for the named player's dominant strategy (two options). The asked player always has exactly one strictly dominant action under the stated objective, high or low price (negotiate or accept) equally often.
example: Maria and Priya have just been offered jobs at a hospital. Each can either negotiate the offer or accept it as it is, and the hospital decides the raises from what both of them do. If both negotiate, each gets a raise of $7,800. If only one negotiates, the one who negotiates gets a raise of $8,400 and the one who accepts gets $2,600. If both accept, each gets a raise of $1,000. Each wants the largest raise for themselves and does not care about the other's. What is the dominant strategy for Maria?

summary: Choosing the undominated action in a small game shown as a payoff matrix.
description: A 2x2 or 3x3 game is shown, either as one player's payoff matrix or as a bimatrix with both players' payoffs, and the question asks which action the model or its opponent should play. One action strictly dominates the others, and it is the correct option among that player's two or three actions; when the question asks for the dominated action, no other action is dominated weakly or by a mixture.
example: Below, find your payoff matrix for some game. You are the row player, what action should you play? Action X Action Y Action R 8.83 7.72 Action S 11.83 10.72

summary: Eliminating dominated actions step by step in a 3x3 game.
description: Each question has two parts. Part 0 shows a 3x3 bimatrix game and asks which of one player's actions is dominated; part 1 asks which of the other player's actions should not be played once that action is removed. Both parts have one correct action.
example: Below, find the payoff matrix for some game. You are the column player, which means the second number in the cell is your payoff and the first number is your opponent's payoff. Which one of your actions is dominated? [3x3 payoff matrix; part 1: Which action should your opponent not play?]

summary: Finding the pure-strategy Nash equilibrium of a game that has exactly one.
description: Three kinds of question, each built from a payoff table generated first. Matrix questions show a 3x3 payoff matrix (integers 0-19 or decimals below 20) and ask, from the row or the column player's side, for your equilibrium action, your opponent's, or the action pair. Pricing stories: two shops each charge a low or a high price, the story lists how many units each sells in all four price combinations, and profit is price times units sold. Salary stories: two employers each offer a low or a high salary; equal offers split the candidates evenly, otherwise the higher offer hires a stated share, and profit is hires times (value per hire minus salary). Word problems ask for the equilibrium pair (with 'There is no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium' as a wrong option) or one firm's equilibrium action. Every game has exactly one pure equilibrium, with strict best responses, checked by brute force.
example: Page Turners and Literati Lodge are the only two bookstores in a lakeside town. Each can charge either $13.15 or $22.65 per copy of a new bestselling novel. [...] If both charge $13.15, Page Turners sells 391 and Literati Lodge sells 136. Costs are negligible, so each one's profit is its price times the number of copies it sells, and each wants to maximise its own profit. In the pure-strategy Nash equilibrium of this pricing game, what price does Page Turners charge?

summary: Solving a short sequential game by backward induction to decide whether a player should stop or continue.
description: A three-round centipede-style negotiation or treatment decision gives each player's payoff at every stopping point. The question asks whether the first mover should end the game in round one or, in a little over half the questions, whether the second mover should end it in round two. The correct option follows from solving the tree from the last decision back, with each mover maximising their own payoff.
example: Two investors, Alice and Bob, are negotiating a funding round for a startup with the startup's CEO setting the terms. The negotiation will proceed over 3 rounds, with Alice and Bob alternating as the lead negotiator. In the first round of negotiations, Alice can either choose to accept the terms or continue negotiating for better conditions. [...]

summary: Finding subgame-perfect play in a stage game repeated a fixed number of times.
description: A 2x2 or 3x3 bimatrix game is repeated for two, three or four rounds, and the question asks what is played in each round if both players mutually best respond: the model's own actions, its opponent's actions, or the action pairs. The correct option repeats the stage game's Nash equilibrium in every round.
example: Below, find the payoff matrix for some game. You are the row player, which means the first number in the cell is your payoff and the second is your opponents's, what actions should you play in each round if the game repeats for two rounds and you and your opponent are mutually best responding? [3x3 payoff matrix]

summary: Identifying which payoffs an infinitely repeated prisoner's dilemma can sustain: the feasible, individually rational payoffs of the folk theorem, or the equilibrium plans at a stated discount factor.
description: Six fixed stories (petrol-station prices, fishing limits, advertising, oil quotas, data sharing between labs, irrigation) state the payoffs per period of a symmetric prisoner's dilemma in the story's own words (both cooperate, both defect, one of each), in whole thousands of dollars; by the story's labels the payoffs always form a genuine prisoner's dilemma. In folk questions no discount factor is given. The question asks which pair of long-run average payoffs is feasible (a long-run average of the four outcomes) and individually rational (above the mutual-defection payoff), or, in the other wording, which pair the folk theorem says a subgame-perfect equilibrium can sustain when both players are very patient. Exactly one option qualifies; the others are infeasible or not individually rational (at least one of each). In discount questions a discount factor and grim-trigger punishment (both defect forever after any departure) are stated, and the options are four repeating plans (cooperate every period; take turns defecting; cooperate and defect in alternate periods; two periods of cooperation, then one of defection; a three-period cycle; one player always cooperating while the other alternates). Exactly one is a subgame-perfect equilibrium at the stated discount factor, which is at least 0.02 from every plan's threshold.
example: Two fishing companies, Company A and Company B, share a lake. Every season each company either keeps to the agreed catch limit or overfishes. If both keep to the catch limit, each earns $82,000 per season; if both overfish, each earns $74,000 per season; if one overfishes while the other keeps to the catch limit, the one that overfishes earns $92,000 and the other earns $51,000 per season. The companies interact in this way every season, forever, and discount the future by a factor of 0.63 per season. Suppose they agree on a plan for every season, and that if either one ever departs from it, both will overfish in every later season. Exactly one of the following plans can be sustained this way as a subgame-perfect equilibrium (no company ever gains by departing from it). Which one? [options: Both keep to the catch limit in every season. / Both keep to the catch limit for two seasons, then both overfish for one season, and this three-season pattern repeats. / They take turns: in the first season Company A overfishes while Company B keeps to the catch limit, in the next season Company B overfishes while Company A keeps to the catch limit, and so on, alternating. / Both keep to the catch limit in the first season, both overfish in the next, and so on, alternating.; key Both keep to the catch limit in every season.]

summary: Deciding which outcome of a repeated prisoner's dilemma can be sustained in equilibrium at a given discount factor.
description: Two firms play a repeated prisoner's dilemma with stated payoffs and discount factor. Options describe outcome paths: both cooperate, both defect, one always defects, players take turns (each period one defects while the other cooperates, swapping roles every period), or none of these. The keyed option is the one path that is a subgame-perfect equilibrium with grim-trigger reversion to mutual defection at that discount factor.
example: Consider two software companies, A and B, engaged in a long-term contract for codevelopment of a product. [...] Given a discount factor of 0.15, if both companies honor the contract, each earns $83645.44 annually; if both breach the contract, each earns $71525.07 annually; [...] which outcome is enforceable as a Nash equilibrium?

summary: Computing the minimum discount factor at which grim-trigger cooperation is subgame perfect in a repeated prisoner's dilemma.
description: A stage game with payoffs R (both cooperate), S and T (one defects) and P (both defect) is given, as a story or a matrix. The correct option is the threshold (T - R) / (T - P), rounded to two decimals as the question asks; distractors are other common formulas.
example: In an infinitely repeated game involving two symmetric gamblers deciding between securing a fixed reward and gambling for a chance to double it, what is the minimum discount factor that supports both players using a grim trigger strategy as a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium? The payoff structure for a single round is as follows: [...]

summary: Finding the Bayes-Nash equilibrium of a 2x2 game whose payoffs depend on a random state.
description: The opponent has a private type (Type 1 or Type 2, with stated probabilities) and a 2x2 payoff table per type. The question asks for your action, or for the opponent's action when of a stated type, in the Bayes-Nash equilibrium; games are drawn so that there is exactly one equilibrium (pure, with no ties and no mixed equilibrium).
example: Consider a game with 2 states: State 1, State 2. The probability of state 1 is 0.19 and the probability of state 2 is 0.81. Suppose no player has any information about the state of the game but common knowledge of the states. What is the Bayes-Nash Equilibrium of the game? [two payoff matrices]

display_name: Pareto Efficiency in Social Welfare Functions
setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Checking whether a group decision respects the Pareto principle given everyone's rankings.
description: A group (a book club, a city council, a band, a family, an office team, a school board) ranks two or three alternatives, and the profile is listed as ballot lines such as "12 voters voted for D > K > T". Half the questions report the group's final decision and ask Yes/No whether it satisfies the Pareto efficiency axiom: the answer is No exactly when every member ranks some other alternative above the chosen one (profiles where that differs from one alternative being ranked above it by everyone are not drawn). The other half state a unanimous preference (every member ranks one alternative first) and ask which alternative should be chosen.
example:
A city council is choosing a design for the new park from three designs: Design C, Design F and Design U. Each member ranked the designs, with these results:
16 voters voted for F > C > U
The council's final decision was Design U. Does this decision satisfy the Pareto efficiency axiom?

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Spotting which of four rules that rank the options violates monotonicity: after one option is moved up on some ballots, an option that was ranked below it overtakes it.
description: A group (a book club, a city council, a band, a family, an office team or a school board) tries four unnamed rules that turn the members' ranked ballots into a group ranking of all options, first on one set of ballots and then on the same ballots after some members moved one option up, with nothing else changed. A rule violates monotonicity when an option that the group ranked below the raised option before the change is ranked above it after the change (the paper's definition: society prefers A to B, A is raised in some individual rankings, and A must still be preferred to B). The rules come from real ones (Borda, plurality and Copeland rankings, and the elimination orders of instant runoff and of Coombs' method) and made-up but well-defined ones (fewest last places; most first-or-second places; the two with most first places on top in head-to-head order; the two highest Borda scores on top, ordered by first places; the two with most first places on top, ordered by Borda points). In consequences questions (easier) each option shows one rule's ranking before and after the change; in procedures questions (harder) the rules are described in words and the reader applies them. Exactly one rule violates monotonicity, and in it the raised option keeps or improves its place (it overtakes one option and is overtaken by another), so the violation shows only when the pairs are compared. In consequences questions the four before / after pairs differ, another rule's ranking changes and in another rule the raised option moves up; in procedures questions another listed rule is of a kind that can violate monotonicity but does not on these ballots. Half of the questions state what monotonicity requires.
example:
Priya chairs an office team and is comparing four rules that turn the members' ballots into a group ranking for choosing a venue for its end-of-year lunch. Each member ranks all three venues (H, L and T). In a trial vote the ballots were:
10 members voted L > H > T
10 members voted T > H > L
11 members voted H > T > L
3 members voted L > T > H
8 members voted H > L > T
2 members voted T > L > H
Then the 8 members who voted H > L > T moved L up, so their ballots became L > H > T. Nothing else changed.
Each of the four rules ranked the venues from the first ballots and from the changed ballots, as listed in the options (best first). Which rule violates monotonicity in this example? [options: Rule 2: H > T > L before the change, H > L > T after it / Rule 1: H > L > T before the change, T > L > H after it / Rule 3: H > T > L before the change, L > H > T after it / Rule 4: H > T > L before the change, H > T > L after it; key Rule 1: H > L > T before the change, T > L > H after it]

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Finding which of four rules turns a profile into a social ranking that is not transitive, or the only one that is.
description: A group tries four unnamed rules that decide, for every pair of options, which one the group places above the other. Pairwise rules can produce cycles (pairwise majority; more members ranking one option immediately above the other; majority among the members who rank neither of the two last, or neither of the two first); score rankings cannot (Borda points, first places, fewest last places, first-or-second places). The ballots often contain a Condorcet cycle. In consequences questions (easier) each option lists one rule's verdict on every pair; in procedures questions (harder) the rules are described and the reader works out the verdicts. The intransitive direction asks which rule's verdicts are not a well-defined (transitive) ranking (exactly one is cyclic); the transitive direction says only one is and asks which. In procedures questions the key is never recognisable from the kind of rule alone.
example:
Grace chairs a school board and is comparing four rules that turn the members' ballots into a group ranking for choosing a new logo for the school. Each member ranks all four logos (B, Q, T and V). The ballots are:
5 members voted T > Q > V > B
9 members voted Q > V > B > T
4 members voted T > V > Q > B
8 members voted B > Q > T > V
For every pair of logos, each rule decides which one the group places above the other. The four rules are:
Rule 1: For each pair of logos, the group places one above the other if more members rank it higher.
Rule 2: For each pair of logos, only the members who rank neither of the two first are counted, and the group places one above the other if more of those members rank it higher.
Rule 3: For each pair of logos, the group places one above the other if more members rank it immediately above the other (with nothing in between) than the other way round.
Rule 4: For each pair of logos, only the members who rank neither of the two last are counted, and the group places one above the other if more of those members rank it higher.
On these ballots, the verdicts of only one rule form a well-defined (transitive) ranking of the logos. Which rule is it? [options: Rule 3 / Rule 4 / Rule 1 / Rule 2; key Rule 2]

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Telling a non-dictatorial rule from dictatorships in disguise, from a rule's wording or from its results.
description: A group's three-member committee (each member with a role, an age and, where needed, a registration order) ranks shortlisted options with strict ballots. Describe questions (easy) list four rules: three are dictatorships in disguise (the chair's ballot, the ballot of whoever registered first, the oldest member's ballot with the next one only breaking ties, the secretary's ballot read top to bottom, the alphabetically first member's ballot) and one is not (Borda points, first places or fewest last places, with a stated tie-break). Consequences questions (medium) give three or four meetings with the members' ballots and four unnamed rules' results, and ask which rule cannot be a dictatorship: three rules copied one member every time, the key differs from every member at some meeting. Procedures questions (hard) describe one subtle procedure (e.g. the two youngest decide if they agree, otherwise the oldest; a weighted Borda count with a stated weight and tie-break; a weighted pairwise vote) and ask whether some member's ballot always becomes the committee's ranking, naming the member; half have a dictator.
example:
You are an AI assistant helping a band decide on the rule by which its three-member committee ranks the shortlisted songs when choosing the opening song for its tour. The songs are D, V and Y. The committee members are Ana (the treasurer, age 50), Kofi (the secretary, age 49) and Nina (the chair, age 27). Each member submits a strict ranking of all three songs (no ties). The proposed rule: Each ballot gives 2 points to its first choice, 1 to its second and 0 to its last; the treasurer's ballot counts 3 times and the others once. The songs are ranked by total points, and ties are broken by the treasurer's ballot.
Is this rule a dictatorship, that is, does one fixed member's ballot become the committee's ranking for every possible set of ballots? [options: Yes: Ana's ballot always becomes the committee's ranking / Yes: Kofi's ballot always becomes the committee's ranking / No: no single member's ballot always does / Yes: Nina's ballot always becomes the committee's ranking; key No: no single member's ballot always does]

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Determining the winner of a plurality election from a table of ranked ballots.
description: An election with four or five candidates lists groups of voters and their rankings. The correct option is the candidate with the most first-place votes.
example: In a 4-candidate plurality election Q, G, O, Y, the votes are counted as: - 24 voters voted for O > G > Q - 52 voters voted for G > Q > Y - 20 voters voted for Y > G > Q - 79 voters voted for O > Y > G Who has the most votes?

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Tallying Borda scores from ranked ballots to find the winner or a given place.
description: Groups of voters rank some or all candidates. The question asks which candidate wins, or finishes in a given position, under the Borda count. The question states the scoring: each ballot ranks three candidates, who get n-1, n-2 and n-3 points in order, and a candidate left off a ballot gets 0.
example: In an election with 4 candidates S, Q, V, E, the voters have the following preferences: - 63 voters voted for Q > S > E - 89 voters voted for E > Q > S - 38 voters voted for E > V > Q - 3 voters voted for S > E > V Using the Borda count method, which candidate wins the election?

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Finding the Condorcet winner, the alternative that beats every other in pairwise majority votes, if one exists.
description: Groups of voters rank three to five alternatives. The correct option is the alternative that wins every head-to-head comparison by a strict majority, or "There is no Condorcet winner" (about 25% of items).
example: A small startup is deciding on the theme for their next project with three potential themes: Theme Y, Theme N, Theme H. They compare each theme against each other to make a decision based on the preferences of the entire team: - 29 voters voted for Y > H > N [...] Which option should be chosen according to the Condorcet criterion?

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Finding the winner under Copeland's method: one point for each one-on-one contest won and half a point for each tie.
description: A group (a book club, a city council, a band, a family, an office team or a school board) chooses among three, four or five alternatives. In profile questions the members' full rankings are given as ballot lines; in table questions only the results of the one-on-one comparisons are given. Half of the questions spell out the rule (one point for each one-on-one contest won, half a point for each tie, most points wins), the others only name Copeland's method. The correct option is the alternative with the highest Copeland score, which is always unique. In about 60% of questions that alternative is not a Condorcet winner (it loses or ties a contest), and where possible it is neither the alternative with the most first places nor the Borda winner, so a simpler count does not give the answer. The options are the alternatives.
example: An office team is choosing a venue for its end-of-year lunch from four venues: Venue H, Venue K, Venue Q and Venue T. Each member ranked all the venues, with these results: 8 members voted for T > Q > H > K / 23 members voted for T > K > Q > H / 16 members voted for Q > K > T > H / 19 members voted for K > T > Q > H. The team decides by Copeland's method. Which venue does the team choose? [options: Venue Q / Venue T / Venue H / Venue K; key Venue K]

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Computing the outcome of a named fair division procedure, or checking an allocation for envy-freeness and proportionality.
description: Each question names the procedure and gives additive valuations. Divide and choose: a 12-inch cake or a 60-metre strip of land is one kind up to a stated point and another after it, both people value each kind at a stated price per unit; the question asks where the divider cuts, which piece the chooser takes and what it is worth to the chooser, or what the divider's piece is worth to the divider. Last diminisher: three or four people, a cake of three flavour sections with each person's points; who gets the first piece and where it ends, or the final allocation (three people). Adjusted winner: two people spread 100 points over 4 to 6 items of an estate or a business; which item is split and the shares (distractors: the shares swapped, an even split, the leader's points only, another item split). Envy check: three people, 4 or 5 items, a proposed allocation; whether it is envy-free and proportional, proportional only, or neither.
example:
You are an AI assistant helping Ivo and Lena divide the family estate. Each of them spreads 100 points over the items:
Watch: Ivo 18, Lena 32
Piano: Ivo 15, Lena 44
Cottage: Ivo 1, Lena 9
Painting: Ivo 24, Lena 11
Stamp collection: Ivo 42, Lena 4
They use the adjusted winner procedure: each item first goes to whoever gives it more points; then the person with more points hands items over to the other, starting with the item for which the ratio of their own points to the other's points is smallest, and splits the item at which the totals would cross, so that both end with the same number of points. Which item is split, and how? [options: The watch is split: Lena keeps 38% of it and Ivo gets 62% / The watch is split: Lena keeps 50% of it and Ivo gets 50% / The piano is split: Lena keeps 62% of it and Ivo gets 38% / The watch is split: Lena keeps 62% of it and Ivo gets 38%; key The watch is split: Lena keeps 62% of it and Ivo gets 38%]

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Judging whether an auction, public-project, facility-location or matching rule, described in words, makes truthful reporting a dominant strategy for every participant.
description: A rule is described in words, never named, and the question states its assumptions: each participant alone knows their own value, favourite spot or ranking; where money changes hands, each cares only about what they get minus what they pay; on a line, nearer is better; rankings are strict. The question asks Yes/No whether reporting truthfully (bidding one's value, staying in a rising-price sale until the price reaches it, accepting a posted price exactly when it is worth it, reporting one's true value, spot or ranking) is a dominant strategy for every participant. Selling one item to three to five bidders: the highest bid wins and pays the best competing bid (Yes), the same with a minimum price announced in advance (Yes), a rising price with final, public drop-outs (Yes), a price fixed in advance (Yes), the winner pays their own bid (No), the third-highest bid (No), everyone pays their bid (No), a draw with chances proportional to the bids (No). A shared purchase split among three to five people: bought when the reported values cover the cost, with equal shares and a fee for a report that changes the decision equal to the others' net loss (Yes), the cost split in proportion to the reports (No), equal shares with no fee (No). A facility placed on a road: the middle report (Yes) or the average (No). Matching: a random order in which each takes their favourite remaining object (Yes), swaps along cycles of people pointing to the owner of their favourite object (Yes), school seats given to first choices first and for good (No), and proposals held and rejected until no one is rejected, asked about the proposing side (Yes) or the receiving side (No). Nine Yes and nine No mechanisms with the same number of questions. For the sealed-bid rules with an outcome fixed by the bids, about a third of the questions add a part with stated bids that asks for the winner and payment, the seller's revenue or a bidder's payoff. A further type gives favourite spots on the road and asks whether a named resident could get the facility closer by reporting a spot further east, further west, or not at all.
example: The three teachers (the teachers at a high school) are deciding whether to buy a coffee machine for the staff room, which costs $1,470. Each teacher reports a value, and the coffee machine for the staff room is bought exactly when the reports add up to at least $1,470; if it is, the cost is shared equally, $490 each. Then, for each teacher, take the others' reports minus their $490 shares and add them up: that total alone would have bought it if it is zero or more, and not otherwise. If the actual decision is different from that one, the teacher pays a fee equal to the size of the total, ignoring its sign. Each teacher alone knows how much the coffee machine for the staff room is worth to them in dollars, and cares only about that value (if it is bought) minus whatever they pay. Under this rule, is it a dominant strategy for each teacher to report exactly what the coffee machine for the staff room is worth to them, whatever the others report? [options: Yes / No; key Yes]

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Judging whether truthful reporting is a Bayes-Nash equilibrium of a mechanism described in words, and finding the first-price equilibrium bid.
description: Values are private and independent, with a stated uniform distribution, and participants are risk-neutral. A seller (an art gallery, a city, a farmer, a charity) or a group deciding on a shared project (residents, employees, parents, a rowing club) uses a mechanism that is described but not named. Yes: second-price sealed bids, a rising price clock with announced drop-outs, a report-based posted price, the expected-externality (AGV) public project, and a winner paying (n-1)/n of their own report; No: first-price and third-price sealed bids, a project paid by pledges, cost shares proportional to reports, and a winner paying another fraction. The last two Yes cases are Bayesian but not dominant-strategy incentive compatible, which separates this element from dsic_mechanism. Yes and No are equally common. A second type asks for a bidder's symmetric equilibrium bid in a first-price auction, (n-1)/n of the value.
example: The parents at Oakridge Elementary are deciding whether to fund a shaded play area. There are four parents. Each parent's value for a shaded play area is private; the values are independent and uniformly distributed between $0 and $950, everyone is risk-neutral, and all of this is common knowledge. The decision rule: Each parent pledges an amount. If the pledges add up to at least the cost of $1,750, the project goes ahead and each parent pays exactly the amount they pledged (anything above the cost goes to a reserve fund); otherwise nothing is built and nobody pays. Is it a Bayes-Nash equilibrium for every parent to pledge exactly their own value? [options: Yes / No; key No]

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Checking whether each participant is better off joining a cost-sharing scheme than staying out.
description: Residents with stated values share the cost of a public good under a stated rule (equal split, shares proportional to usage, a nonzero outside option, or VCG). The question asks who would be better off not participating. The correct option is the person whose value minus payment is below their outside option, or "Everyone is better off participating".
example: Four neighbors on Birch Street are deciding on a shared tool library costing $140. Values: Max $160, Ines $95, Yara $20 and Jo $60. Rule: The cost is split equally, so each of the four pays the same share. [...] Which neighbor would be better off not participating?

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Checking whether a payment scheme collects exactly the cost (strong budget balance) or at least the cost (weak budget balance) of a shared project, under the convention the question states.
description: A group funds a project either with equal cost shares plus stated fees, credits or Clarke taxes, or (about a third of questions) with individually stated payments and rebates. Every question states which of the two conventions "budget balanced" means: strong budget balance (the money collected equals the cost exactly; a surplus or a deficit is not balanced) or weak budget balance (no deficit; a surplus is allowed). The two are equally common. Each of the four options gives a balance status, labelled by the stated convention, and the size of any surplus or deficit; the correct one is the scheme's actual balance.
example: A new drum set for five band members at Lincoln Middle School will cost $900. Each person pays an equal share of the cost. In addition, Pia pays a $60 administration fee into the same fund. Also, Nia, Aiko, Ines and Tess each receive a $15 setup-help credit paid out of the fund. [...] Is it budget balanced?

setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Running the Top Trading Cycles algorithm to find who ends up with which item.
description: Three to five people each own one item (household items, books, sports gear, collectibles or musical instruments) and rank all the items, their own included, best first ("Ana owns the lamp and ranks the items: clock > vase > lamp"). Four kinds of question, four options each (three when only three items can be listed): the final allocation (distractors include serial dictatorship in the listed or reversed order and the first round's trades alone); the trading cycle that forms in the first round (drawn so that exactly one cycle of two or more people forms); whether a proposed final allocation is the outcome ("Yes", or one of three "No, the outcome is: ..." options; the proposal is right in half of the questions); and which item one person ends up with. At least one trade happens in every question. The swap is anonymous, run by the reader as an AI assistant, or, for the last kind, the reader is one of the traders.
example:
A few neighbours swap books using the Top Trading Cycles algorithm. Each owns one item and ranks all the items, best first:
Ivo owns the atlas and ranks the items: almanac > atlas > anthology
Ben owns the anthology and ranks the items: almanac > atlas > anthology
Dev owns the almanac and ranks the items: atlas > almanac > anthology
Which trading cycle forms in the first round of Top Trading Cycles? [options: Ivo gets the almanac, Dev gets the atlas / Ivo gets the almanac, Ben gets the atlas, Dev gets the anthology / Ivo gets the anthology, Ben gets the almanac, Dev gets the atlas / Ben gets the almanac, Dev gets the anthology]

display_name: Optimal Auction for Bidders with Differing Risk Attitudes
setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Choosing the revenue-maximising auction format given bidders' risk attitudes, and computing equilibrium bids and revenue.
description: Three types. risk_ranking asks a seller to choose between two auction formats when bidders are risk-averse (first-price or Dutch earns more), risk-neutral (same revenue) or risk-seeking (second-price or English earns more). expected_revenue and equilibrium_bid use independent uniform private values: expected revenue V(n-1)/(n+1) and first-price bid v(n-1)/n.
example: Seven risk-neutral collectors want a vintage wristwatch. Values are private and drawn independently from a uniform distribution between $0 and $504. If the jeweler runs a Dutch (descending-price) auction with no reserve price, what revenue should it expect in equilibrium?

display_name: Optimal Auction for Bidders with Affiliated Values
setting: Decisions on Behalf of Other Agents
summary: Ranking auction formats by expected revenue when the value environment has to be read from the story.
description: Eight stories: four with a common resale value and private noisy estimates (an oil tract with separate seismic surveys, returned laptops tested in different handfuls, a wine lot for resale, a forest tract surveyed in parts), two with independent private values (a chef's dinner, a walk-on role) and two with private values and cautious bidders who strictly prefer a gamble's average for sure to the gamble. The environment is never named, and each story has an explicit and a subtle wording of its cues; every story also states the information structure (estimates as noisy signals of one value, strictly affiliated with it, or values each bidder already knows), symmetric bidders, equilibrium bidding and no reserve. The formats are described, not named (a rising price clock with announced drop-outs, second-price and first-price sealed bids, a falling price clock) and labelled Format 1 to 4. Ranking questions ask for the order of three or four formats by expected revenue, ties included (affiliated: rising clock > second-price > first-price = falling clock; private values: all equal; cautious bidders: first-price = falling clock > second-price = rising clock). Information-policy questions ask whether the seller should commit to publishing an independent appraisal (yes under affiliation, no difference otherwise).
example:
You are an AI assistant advising the seller in this auction. A football club is auctioning a signed match ball to four fans who want it for their own shelves; how much each fan cares about it is personal and unrelated to the others. The fans are cautious: offered a sure $50 or a coin flip for $100, each of them takes the sure $50. The seller is considering three formats:
Format 1: A price clock starts high and falls; the first bidder to stop it wins and pays the price shown.
Format 2: Each bidder submits a sealed bid; the highest bidder wins and pays their own bid.
Format 3: A price clock starts low and rises; bidders drop out one by one, every drop-out is announced to all, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the previous bidder dropped out.
Rank these formats by the seller's expected revenue, highest first ("=" means equal expected revenue). [options: Format 1 = Format 2 > Format 3 / Format 3 > Format 1 = Format 2 / Format 1 = Format 2 = Format 3 / Format 3 > Format 2 > Format 1; key Format 1 = Format 2 > Format 3]

summary: Differentiating a linear, quadratic or cubic polynomial with respect to x.
description: The question gives a polynomial with decimal coefficients and asks for its derivative. The correct option is the term-by-term derivative; distractors keep a term that should vanish, forget to multiply by the exponent, or keep the old exponent.
example: What is the derivative of the following function with respect to x, 1.26x^2 + 9.77x + 8.34?

summary: Raising a decimal number to a whole or fractional power.
description: A bare calculation, in five phrasings: a base with two decimals between 1.1 and 9.99 raised to a whole exponent from 2 to 6 (type integer) or to a fractional exponent with two decimals between 0.25 and 3.5 (type real_value). The correct option is the power rounded to two decimals. The other options come from common mistakes: the base times the exponent, one power too few or too many, the exponent taken as a root, or the exponent raised to the base. This is one of the STEER-ME Foundations elements: the STEER-ME paper reports that foundational competence predicts downstream performance.
example: A calculation requires the value of 1.86^2. What is it, rounded to two decimals? [options: 6.43 / 1.36 / 3.72 / 3.46; key 3.46]

summary: Solving two linear equations in x and y, or three in x, y and z.
description: A bare system of two equations in x and y (type two_equation) or three in x, y and z (type three_equation), in five phrasings, with whole coefficients from -9 to 9 and a whole-number solution. The options are whole-number assignments to the unknowns. The correct option is the solution; the others are the solution with the values swapped (or rotated), a point that satisfies every equation except the last, the solution with every sign flipped, or the solution with one value off by one.
example: Two quantities x and y must satisfy these conditions simultaneously: 6x - 8y = -112 / -6x - 5y = 8. What are their values? [options: x = 8, y = -8 / x = -16, y = 2 / x = -8, y = 7 / x = -8, y = 8; key x = -8, y = 8]

summary: Predicting the direction of a quantity (or price) change implied by the law of demand.
description: A price change is stated and the question asks for the most likely new quantity demanded, or a quantity change is stated and it asks for the price that caused it. Exactly one option lies on the side the law of demand predicts (price up, quantity down, and conversely); the three distractors lie on the other side. The question states that nothing else affecting demand has changed (a movement along one downward-sloping demand curve) and that exactly one option is consistent with that; stories that describe a demand shift (popularity, trends), a quantity that is not the quantity demanded (stock, procedures performed, quantities sold or used, or never called demand), a yield or interest rate as the price, or that state the direction of the asked value are not used.
example: Maria is considering the demand for a new health supplement. Initially, when the price is 165.19, the quantity demanded is 3. If the price of the supplement decreases to 65.09, what is the most likely new quantity demanded?

summary: Computing the price elasticity of demand from a price change and the resulting quantity change.
description: Starting and ending prices and quantities are given for a good or service. The correct option is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price, both measured from the starting values (a negative number).
example: I noticed that when the price of a specialized treatment at our clinic increased from 12.85 to 32.06, the number of patients opting for the treatment decreased from 38.2 to 13.49. What is the price elasticity of demand for this treatment?

summary: Deriving the Engel curve of a good, the income at which a consumer buys each quantity, from a Cobb-Douglas utility and prices.
description: A consumer (the consumers of Duality of Hicksian Demand) spends all income on two goods, with a utility written either as x^a * y^b or as a ln(x) + b ln(y) (the same preferences) and fixed prices. Types: which equation m = c x is the Engel curve of good x, or m = c y of good y (the key is c = (1 + b/a) px, or (1 + a/b) py); and how many more units of x the consumer buys when income rises by a stated amount (a/(a+b) times the rise, divided by px). The other options come from common mistakes: the exponent ratio inverted, the other good's price, all income spent on the good, the exponent used as the budget share, or the other good's share.
example: Kenji buys financial planning (good x) and investing courses (good y) and spends all of Kenji's income m on them. Kenji's utility is U(x, y) = 0.2 ln(x) + 0.55 ln(y), where x is the number of financial-planning sessions and y the number of investing courses per year. The price of financial planning is $12 per session and the price of investing courses is $9 per course, and both can be bought in any fractional amount. Prices stay fixed. Which equation is the Engel curve for investing courses, giving the income m per year at which Kenji buys y investing courses? [options: m = 9y / m = 16.36y / m = 33.75y / m = 12.27y; key m = 12.27y]

summary: Computing an income elasticity of demand from percentage changes, or using one to predict a change in quantity or income.
description: A consumer (the consumers and goods of Duality of Hicksian Demand) faces unchanged prices. Types: direct (income changed from one stated amount to another and the quantity bought from one number to another; the key is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in income, each measured from the original value; about a quarter of the goods are inferior, with a negative elasticity); quantity (the elasticity and a percentage rise in income are given; the key is the percentage change in quantity, the product); income (the elasticity and a percentage change in quantity are given; the key is the percentage change in income, the quotient). The other options come from common mistakes: the ratio inverted, the midpoint formula, the slope instead of the elasticity, changes measured from the new values, or the elasticity and the change added, multiplied instead of divided or taken as a fraction rather than a percentage; in half the questions the key and one mistake also appear with the sign flipped (two +/- pairs), otherwise no option is a sign flip.
example: When your income changed from $2,400 to $3,400 a year, with prices unchanged, you changed your purchases of financial planning from 96 to 118 financial-planning sessions a year. Measuring each percentage change from the original value, what is your income elasticity of demand for financial planning? Round to two decimals. [options: 0.63 / 0.55 / -0.55 / 0.02; key 0.55]

summary: Predicting how the share of income spent on a good changes when its price rises, from a CES utility with a stated elasticity of substitution.
description: A consumer (the consumers of Duality of Hicksian Demand) spends all income on two goods. The utility is CES, U = (a x^ρ + b y^ρ)^(1/ρ) with a + b = 1, or Cobb-Douglas, and the elasticity of substitution σ = 1/(1 - ρ) is stated (σ = 1 for Cobb-Douglas). The price of x rises by 10% to 60%. Types: direction (does the share of income spent on x rise, fall or stay the same? It rises when σ < 1, stays the same when σ = 1 and falls when σ > 1; a third of the questions each) and new_share (the share of income spent on x after the rise, in percent). The other options of new_share come from common mistakes: the old share, the quantity of x left unchanged, the old share divided by the price rise, the share of y, or the share after a price fall. The paper's definition also mentions Giffen goods; that half is left out, since it has no determinate answer without a specific Giffen utility.
example: Kenji spends all of Kenji's income of $1,670 a year on financial planning (good x) and investing courses (good y). Kenji's utility is U(x, y) = (a * x^ρ + b * y^ρ)^(1/ρ) with a = 0.7, b = 0.3 and ρ = -1, where x is the number of financial-planning sessions and y the number of investing courses per year; this is a CES (constant elasticity of substitution) utility function, whose elasticity of substitution between the two goods is σ = 0.5. The price of financial planning is $34 per session and the price of investing courses is $29 per course, and both can be bought in any fractional amount.
